paragraphs.text: Lesson 35, Certainty and Probability
Karen and Linda made plans to go shopping one night at 7pm.
Karen is at Linda's house, but Linda isn't there, so Karen calls Linda's brother Eric to ask for information.
Listen to their conversation to learn phrases for expressing certainty and probability.
Hi, Eric, it's Karen. Do you know where Linda is?
I'm pretty sure she's at home. How come?
Well, I'm at her house right now. She asked me to pick her up so that we could do some shopping together.
I'm positive she told me to come at 7, but nobody's answering the door.
She could have gone out.
That's unlikely. She told me she'd be at home all evening.
Maybe she's in the shower?
That's what I thought, too, but I've been ringing her doorbell for the past 15 minutes.
Well, have you tried her cell phone?
Yes, no answer.
Are you dialing the right number? She changed her number recently.
It's definitely the right number. She gave it to me yesterday.
It's possible that she simply forgot you were coming and made other plans.
I'd be very surprised. Linda's not the type of person to forget, and I have no doubt she would have called me if something else had come up.
Then she must still be on her way home from work.
Yeah, I guess she's stuck in traffic or something.
Hang on a second. It looks like I've got an email from her.
Apparently she's still in a meeting and she accidentally left her cell phone at home.
She asked me to call you and tell you that there's not much chance of her leaving the office before eight.
Oh, okay. Thanks for letting me know.
Conversation Vocabulary and Phrases
In this dialogue, Karen and Eric discuss various possibilities about where Linda is at the moment.
Some things they are certain about and other things they are not completely certain about, so they need to guess.
If you are 100% certain that something is true, you can say,
I'm certain that or I'm quite certain that,
I'm positive that or I'm absolutely positive that,
I have no doubt that. It's definitely.
Sometimes to support a statement you want to use external evidence like popular agreement or scientific facts.
For example, it's common knowledge that everybody knows that.
It's no secret that few people would deny that.
It's a well-established fact that it has been proven that if you make a logical deduction that you are certain is true or correct,
you can use must for situations in the present or must have for situations in the past.
For example, there's no signal on my cell phone. We must be out of range of a cell phone tower.
Her car isn't here. She must have gone out.
Now, if you are mostly certain about something but not 100%, you can say,
I'm pretty sure, as Eric says in the dialogue, I'm pretty sure she's at home.
When you're not sure about something, you can guess or imagine the possibilities or probabilities.
These phrases are used for guessing with a strong degree of certainty.
There's a good chance. The odds are, probably, it's likely or it's very likely.
I bet. And these phrases are used for guessing with less certainty.
I guess. It seems that it's possible. I wouldn't be surprised if.
We can also use the words might and could for possibilities in the present or future,
and might have and could have for possibilities in the past.
For example, it might rain tomorrow. The floor is wet. There might be a leak in the refrigerator,
or someone might have spilled some water. If your computer isn't working properly,
it could be infected with a virus. I could have gotten a better job if I had studied harder in school.
To say that something is not probable, use these phrases. It's unlikely. Or it's not likely.
There's not much hope. Or there's not much chance. I'd be very surprised if, plus past participle.
For example, I'd be very surprised if that team won the championship next week.
We use the past participle in this structure, even though the event is in the future.
I don't expect, plus two and a verb. For example, I don't expect that team to win the championship next week.
Finally, to say something is not possible at all, use these phrases. It's impossible.
There's no chance that. That would never happen. That couldn't have happened.
The phrase that couldn't have happened is only for things in the past. That can't be true.
You can use can't for the present and future, and couldn't have in the past to express impossibilities.
For example, you can't buy beer. You're only fifteen. Steve couldn't have bought the beer. He's only fifteen.
An older friend must have bought it for him. As you can see, can't have is used for the impossible part.
Which is, fifteen-year-old Steve buying the beer. And must have is used for the probable or certain part.
Which is, an older friend buying the beer for Steve. For additional clarification on the topics of May and might,
as well as could have, should have, and would have, check out the lessons which are linked in the lesson text.
